presentation.title: Why I Do Not Believe Christianity Is True

slide.title: Cover
Why I Do Not Believe Christianity Is True
slide.subtitle: An evidence-based look at the claims of Christianity through the lenses of science, history, Jesus, morality, scripture, and philosophy.
slide.notes: Welcome. Today we're going to examine the central question: is Christianity true? Not whether it's comforting or culturally significant, but whether its truth claims hold up to scrutiny. We'll go through six evidence areas: scientific, historical, Jesus's claims, moral philosophy, the Bible itself, and broader philosophical questions. Each part builds on the last.

slide.title: Section Intro
Setting the Ground Rules
slide.subtitle: Before we begin, we need to establish what we're actually arguing about and who carries the burden.
slide.notes: Before we dive into the arguments, we need to be clear on the rules of engagement. What exactly are we debating? And who has the burden of proof? These aren't rhetorical tricks -- they're necessary framing that prevents talking past each other.

slide.title: Burden of Proof
Burden of Proof
slide.subtitle: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: Christianity makes positive claims about reality: a God exists, Jesus rose from the dead, prayers are answered, miracles occur. These are not neutral statements -- they assert something extraordinary about the universe.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: Whoever makes a positive claim carries the burden of proof. Skepticism is not a counter-claim -- it's the default position until sufficient evidence is presented. The lack of belief is not a belief in lack.

slide.notes: The most common confusion in these debates: atheism isn't the claim that "no god exists" with certainty. It's the lack of belief in the god claim due to insufficient evidence. The difference matters. If I tell you there's a dragon in my garage, you don't have to prove there isn't -- I have to show you the dragon.

slide.title: Evidence That Matters
Evidence That Matters
slide.subtitle: Christianity makes testable claims about the world. We'll examine six independent evidence areas -- each acts as a lens that reveals whether those claims hold up.

card.title: No Faith Required
card.content: These are all secular, evidence-based inquiries. No scripture, no dogma, no theological assumptions -- just the same tools we use to evaluate any truth claim about the world.

card.title: Six Chances to Be Right
card.content: If Christianity is true, it should hold up in **at least one** of these areas -- ideally all six. If it fails in every single one, that is not a coincidence. That's a pattern.

slide.notes: The reason to use six independent evidence areas is to eliminate special pleading. A Christian can't retreat to "you just need faith" when science contradicts the Bible -- because we're also testing history, Jesus's claims, morality, the biblical text itself, and philosophy. The Bible section also addresses common defense arguments. If all six point the same direction, the pattern is clear.

slide.title: The Six Lines
Six Lines of Evidence
slide.subtitle: We'll evaluate Christianity on six independent lines of evidence. Each stands on its own; together they form a cumulative case.

card.title: 🔬 Scientific
card.content: Evolution, geology, and genetics contradict a literal Genesis. Every line of evidence points to an ancient Earth and common descent.

card.title: 📜 Historical
card.content: Archaeology fails to confirm the Bible's foundational stories: no Exodus, no conquest of Canaan, no Davidic empire.

card.title: ✝️ Jesus
card.content: The resurrection lacks credible evidence; OT prophecies were retrofitted; Jesus's own predictions of his return went unfulfilled.

card.title: ⚖️ Moral
card.content: Hell and original sin are morally indefensible. The Bible endorses slavery, genocide, and misogyny.

card.title: 📖 Biblical
card.content: The Bible is riddled with contradictions, the canon was decided by men with agendas, and inerrancy is an indefensible position.

card.title: 🧠 Philosophical
card.content: Faith is not a virtue, Pascal's Wager is a logical trap, the problem of evil remains unanswered, and divine hiddenness undermines claims of a personal God.

slide.notes: These six lines of evidence are largely independent. Even if the scientific case were weak, the historical and moral arguments might still be compelling -- or vice versa. We'll examine each on its own merits and then see how they stack up together.

slide.title: Section Scientific
The Scientific Argument
slide.subtitle: Does science point toward or away from the Christian worldview?
slide.notes: The scientific argument is often the starting point. Christians point to fine-tuning, the origin of life, and the complexity of biology as evidence for a creator. Critics point to evolution, geology, and cosmology as evidence against a literal reading of scripture and as natural explanations for what religion once attributed to God.

slide.title: Scientific Intro
The God of the Gaps
slide.subtitle: Science has a history of closing gaps where God was once the only explanation. The scientific evidence against a literal Genesis is not a recent discovery -- it is the culmination of centuries of inquiry.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: Lightning = physics. Disease = germ theory. The origin of species = evolution. The pattern is unmistakable: every domain once attributed to divine action now has a natural explanation. This section tests Christianity's specific claims against science: young Earth, special creation, global flood, and a single human pair.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: This section examines Christianity's specific claims about the natural world: that the Earth is young, that species were individually created, that a global flood reshaped the planet, that humans arose from a single pair. In each case, the scientific evidence tells a different story. The question is not whether Christianity can accommodate science -- it can, through reinterpretation. The question is whether the evidence supports a literal reading of Genesis, and what that means for a faith built on that foundation.

slide.notes: The God of the Gaps argument is the most common but also the weakest. It says "science can't explain X, therefore God." The problem is that historically, every time we've said that, science eventually does explain X. Lightning, disease, the motions of the planets, the origin of species -- all were once attributed to God, all now have natural explanations. This section covers what science actually tells us about the specific claims Christianity makes about the natural world.

slide.title: Did God Create
Did God Create the Universe?

card.title: The Claim
card.content:
The Kalam Cosmological Argument is one of the most popular intellectual defenses of theistic belief. It attempts to prove that the universe must have been caused by a creator. Here's how it works:
- Whatever begins to exist has a cause. - The universe began to exist. - Therefore, the universe has a cause. - That cause is God.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - Special pleading: If everything that begins needs a cause, what caused God? If God doesn't need a cause, why can't the universe be the uncaused thing? - Equivocation: Even if premise 3 is granted, the conclusion "that cause is God" smuggles in attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, benevolence) that aren't in the premises. The cause could be a quantum fluctuation, a multiverse bubble, or anything else.

card.title: The bottom line:
card.content: The Kalam argument commits special pleading for God. If everything that begins needs a cause, what caused God? If God doesn't need a cause, why can't the universe be the uncaused thing? And even if there is a first cause, nothing in the argument shows it's the God of the Bible -- it could be a quantum fluctuation, a multiverse bubble, or something we haven't discovered yet. The argument smuggles in theology where it only has cosmology.

slide.notes: The Kalam argument has been popularized by William Lane Craig, but it has a fatal flaw: it treats God as a special exception to its own logic. If the universe needs a cause because it began to exist, then God -- who is also said to be a conscious being with a beginning (though theologians dispute this) -- would need one too. And if you say "God is eternal, he didn't begin," then you've simply moved the mystery back one step. Why not stop at the universe?

slide.title: Did God Design
Did God Design the Universe?
slide.subtitle: "The universe appears designed. Therefore a designer exists."

card.title: The Claim
card.content: Physical constants (gravitational constant, cosmological constant, strong nuclear force, etc.) appear to be finely tuned to within extraordinarily narrow ranges. If any were even slightly different, life could not exist. This seems to suggest a fine-tuner.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: 1. The Anthropic Principle -- we can only observe a universe that permits our existence. 2. The multiverse hypothesis -- if there are countless universes with varying constants, ours being life-permitting is unremarkable. 3. Fine-tuning assumes life is the goal -- why not fine-tuned for something else?

**The Puddle Analogy:** A puddle waking up thinking **"What a wonderful hole -- it fits me perfectly!"** mistakes its shape for evidence the hole was designed for it. We observe a universe that permits our existence -- that's not surprising, it's tautological.

card.title: The bottom line
card.content: The fine-tuning argument sounds compelling until you realize it's a puddle admiring the hole it fits into. We exist in a universe that permits our existence because we couldn't exist in any other. That's not evidence of design -- it's a tautology. And with no proof of a multiverse, the argument remains untestable. A designer is one possible explanation, but far from the simplest one.

slide.notes: The fine-tuning argument sounds compelling until you examine it closely. We exist in a universe that permits our existence -- that's not surprising, it's tautological.

slide.title: Age of the Earth
Did God Create the Earth 6,000 Years Ago?
slide.subtitle: A direct contradiction between scripture and every dating method.

card.title: The Claim
card.content:
Adding up Genesis genealogies yields a specific age for the Earth. Archbishop James Ussher calculated **4004 BCE** for creation (~**6,000 years** ago). The Septuagint gives a slightly older figure of **~10,000 years**. Either way, the Bible places the Earth at thousands of years old -- a specific, testable claim grounded in the plain reading of the text.
~10,000 years

card.title: 🌌 Stellar Distance
card.content:
Light from galaxies billions of light-years away reaches us. A 6,000-year-old universe would mean God created light in transit -- a deceptive appearance of age.
13.8 billion years

card.title: ⛰️ Radiometric Dating
card.content:
Uranium-lead dating of zircon crystals gives Earth at **4.4 billion years**. Multiple independent methods (K-Ar, Rb-Sr, Sm-Nd, U-Pb) all agree.
4.4 billion years

card.title: 🪨 Geological Column
card.content:
Globally consistent rock layers with distinct fossils. Makes no sense in a 6,000-year timeframe -- requires rejecting the entire edifice of modern geology.
4.5 billion years

card.title: The bottom line:
card.content: Every independent dating method in science -- radiometric, geological, astronomical -- agrees on a 4.5-billion-year-old Earth. The biblical figure of 6,000--10,000 years is contradicted by every branch of science that measures age. To accept the Bible's timeline, you must reject the entire edifice of modern geology, physics, and astronomy.

slide.notes: This is perhaps the most straightforward contradiction. If you take the Bible literally, the Earth is at most 10,000 years old. Every scientific discipline that measures age -- astronomy, geology, physics, biology -- independently arrives at 4.5 billion years. You can reconcile this by saying Genesis isn't literal, but then you have to explain which parts are literal and which aren't, and on what basis you decide.

slide.title: Evolution Summary
Evolved, Not Created
slide.subtitle: Evolution is the cornerstone of modern biology -- supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: God created the animals, plants, and all living things "according to their kinds" in six literal days (Genesis 1). Each species was created separately and fixed -- evolution from one form into another is not how life arose. This is the foundation of creationism: special creation, not common descent.

card.title: 🦴 Fossil Record: Every Prediction Confirmed
card.content: Evolution makes testable predictions -- every one confirmed. Tiktaalik (fish with wrist bones) found exactly where predicted. Feathered dinosaurs closed the bird-reptile gap. The complete whale series exists, from wolf-like land mammal to fully aquatic giant, each stage in the right strata. If creationism were true, none of these sequences should exist.

card.title: 🧪 Caught in the Act
card.content: We watch evolution happen. Bacteria evolve antibiotic resistance in real time. Darwin's finches change beak shape in droughts. Italian wall lizards evolved new gut structures in 36 years. Ring species like Ensatina salamanders show one species becoming two -- observable, testable, repeatable science.

card.title: 🩻 Bad Design: The Signature of Evolution
card.content: The recurrent laryngeal nerve takes a 4.5-meter detour around the giraffe's aorta; in fish it's direct, trapped as necks lengthened. Our eyes are wired backwards with a blind spot; the octopus eye got it right. The vas deferens loops over the ureter. An intelligent engineer wouldn't design any of this. Evolution tinkering with existing structures would.

card.title: The bottom line:
card.content: Evolution is one of the most thoroughly tested theories in science. It does not disprove God, but it makes a **literal reading of Genesis impossible**. No Adam and Eve, no original sin, no Fall, no special creation. Christian soteriology has no foundation. **See Appendix** for the full evidence.

slide.notes: Forceful summary of evolution evidence for casual readers. Key message: evolution is settled science that makes a literal Genesis impossible.

slide.title: Origin of Humankind
Origin of Humankind: The Evidence for Common Descent
slide.subtitle: Did humans evolve from apes? The evidence says yes -- overwhelmingly so, across fossils, genetics, and population biology.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: God created mankind in His own image -- Adam from the dust of the ground and Eve from Adam's rib (Genesis 2). Humans are a special creation, uniquely made in God's image, not the product of an evolutionary process from ape-like ancestors. This is the biblical account of human origins.

card.title: The Fossil Record
card.content: The hominin sequence is one of the best-documented transitions in paleontology: **Sahelanthropus** (7 mya) → **Australopithecus** ("Lucy") → **Homo habilis** (tools) → **Homo erectus** (fire) → **Neanderthals** → **Homo sapiens**. The lineage is gradual and precisely dated. No gaps, no missing links.

card.title: Adam & Eve: The Genetic Impossibility
card.content: Population genetics shows humanity never bottlenecked to two individuals. Minimum viable population is 10,000--40,000. Our genetic diversity is far too high for a single pair. Mitochondrial Eve and Y-chromosomal Adam lived tens of thousands of years apart. A literal Adam and Eve is genetically impossible.

card.title: Chromosome 2 Fusion
card.content: Great apes have 48 chromosomes; humans have 46. Human chromosome 2 resulted from two ancestral chromosomes fusing end-to-end, confirmed by two vestigial centromeres and telomere sequences in the middle. Every ape genome has the two separate chromosomes; only humans have the fused version.

slide.notes: Three topics on slide 1: the fossil record demonstrating gradual human evolution, population genetics ruling out a two-person bottleneck, and the chromosome 2 fusion as the first genetic signature of common ancestry. The remaining genetic evidence continues on the next slide.

slide.title: Genetic Evidence
The Genetic Evidence: We Are Apes
slide.subtitle: Our DNA confirms what the fossils suggest -- we share a common ancestor with the great apes.

card.title: Shared Broken Genes
card.content: The GULO gene (vitamin C production) is broken identically in humans, chimps, gorillas, and orangutans by the same mutation. Over 200 processed pseudogenes are shared at identical genomic positions. These are genetic fossils -- broken in the same way in the same places. An intelligent designer has no reason to copy non-functional DNA.

card.title: ERVs: Viral Fossils
card.content: Hundreds of endogenous retrovirus insertions are shared between humans and chimps at the exact same genomic coordinates. When a retrovirus infects a germ cell, its DNA becomes permanent. Shared insertions mean the infection happened in a common ancestor. The odds of independent insertion at the same spot are effectively zero.

card.title: 98.8% Genetic Identity
card.content: Human and chimpanzee genomes are 98.8% identical. The similarity follows a nested hierarchy: we share more with chimps than gorillas, more with gorillas than orangutans. This is exactly what evolution predicts and is inexplicable under independent creation.

card.title: The bottom line
card.content: The genetic evidence alone places humans firmly within the great ape family. Combined with the fossil sequence, the case for common ancestry is as strong as any conclusion in science. A literal Adam and Eve contradicts all of it.

slide.notes: Three more genetic lines of evidence: shared broken genes (pseudogenes), shared ERV insertions, and 98.8% genome-wide identity. Together with slide 1, six independent lines all converge on common ancestry.

slide.title: Scientific Summary
What Science Actually Shows
slide.subtitle: Five Christian claims, five scientific findings -- and what it means for theology.

card.content: **Claim:** God created the universe. **Science:** The universe began with the Big Bang 13.8 billion years ago. Kalam argument fails.
**Claim:** The universe is finely tuned for life. **Science:** Anthropic principle and multiverse hypothesis explain fine-tuning without design.
**Claim:** God created the Earth 6,000 years ago. **Science:** Radiometric dating, stellar distances, and geology all show a 4.5-billion-year-old Earth.
**Claim:** God created species separately. **Science:** Fossil record, observed evolution, and genetic evidence confirm common descent.
**Claim:** God created humans uniquely. **Science:** Fossils, genetics, and chromosome evidence show humans evolved from ape-like ancestors.

card.title: The Verdict
card.content: No Adam means no original sin -- and without original sin, the need for a savior disappears. Paul explicitly ties Christ's redemption to Adam's transgression (Romans 5:12-21). Without the Fall, there is nothing to be saved from. Humans share a common ancestor with every living thing. Death and extinction have been part of life for hundreds of millions of years -- they cannot be the result of Adam's sin. The image of God becomes hard to define when our lineage connects continuously to earlier hominins. Christianity can accommodate evolution by reinterpreting Genesis allegorically, but the theological cost is steep: the core soteriological framework must be abandoned or redefined beyond recognition.

slide.notes: The scientific evidence consistently contradicts a literal reading of Genesis. Every independent line of evidence -- physics, chemistry, geology, biology, genetics -- converges on the same conclusion: the Earth is ancient and life evolved. The Kalam and fine-tuning arguments rely on logical fallacies, not evidence. Evolution doesn't disprove God, but it undermines the specific story Christianity tells about why we need saving and how that salvation works. No Fall, no need for a savior.

slide.title: Section Historical
The Historical Argument
slide.subtitle: Do biblical events hold up when tested against archaeology, geology, and historical evidence?
slide.notes: The Bible presents specific events as literal history: a global flood, an exodus from Egypt, a conquest of Canaan, a united monarchy, and the life and resurrection of Jesus. These claims can be tested against independent evidence. This section examines what archaeology, geology, and historical criticism reveal.

slide.title: Historical Intro
Testing the Bible as History
slide.subtitle: The Bible presents specific events as literal history. What happens when we check the evidence?

card.title: The Claim
card.content: The Old Testament describes a global flood that destroyed all life except Noah's Ark, a mass Exodus of millions of Israelites from Egypt, and a military conquest of Canaan led by Joshua. These are not presented as allegory or metaphor -- they are described as real events that happened to real people in specific places at specific times. If any of them can be shown to be historically false, the Bible's credibility as a historical document is seriously compromised.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: The ancient Near East is one of the most intensively excavated regions in the world. We have extensive records from Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon -- inscriptions, annals, administrative documents, and royal propaganda. We can date pottery, trace settlement patterns, and read the records of the very civilizations the Bible describes. If the Exodus happened, Egypt would have recorded it. If the Conquest happened, the ruins would show it. If Noah's Flood happened, the geology would prove it. This is not a matter of interpretation -- it is a matter of evidence.

slide.notes: This section covers the three most significant cases where archaeology directly contradicts or fails to support the biblical account. These are not fringe positions -- they are the consensus of mainstream archaeology and biblical historiography.

slide.title: Noah's Flood
Noah's Flood: The Geological Impossibility

card.title: The Claim
card.content: According to Genesis, God flooded the entire Earth, covering even the highest mountains, killing every land animal and human not on Noah's Ark. The flood lasted 40 days and nights, and the waters covered the earth for over a year before receding. All modern humanity and land animals are descended from the eight people and the animals on that single boat. This is presented as literal, global history.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - No geological evidence for a global flood in the last 6,000 years - Stratigraphic layers show gradual deposition over millions of years, not a single catastrophic flood - Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica show annual layers going back 100,000+ years — uninterrupted - If a global flood occurred, we'd expect a worldwide layer of flood sediment. No such layer exists. - 8 people could not feed, clean, and care for ~35,000+ animal species (let alone insects and marine life) - Freshwater fish would die in saltwater; saltwater fish in freshwater - Post-flood repopulation is genetically impossible from such a small founder population - Kangaroos and koalas making it from Ararat to Australia without leaving fossils along the way stretches credulity

slide.notes: The Noah's Ark story is one of the most well-known in the Bible, and one of the most empirically falsifiable. Every branch of science -- geology, biology, genetics, archaeology -- independently concludes that no global flood occurred in human history. The story almost certainly derives from older Mesopotamian flood myths like the Epic of Gilgamesh, which predate the Genesis account.

slide.title: The Exodus
The Exodus: The Missing Evidence
slide.subtitle: The foundational story of Israel -- with zero archaeological support.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: The Book of Exodus describes 600,000 Israelite men (likely 2--3 million people total) living as slaves in Egypt, enduring ten plagues, then walking out of Egypt after the firstborn of every Egyptian family was killed. They crossed the Red Sea, wandered in the Sinai desert for 40 years, and received the Law at Mount Sinai. This was a civilization-altering event -- a catastrophe for Egypt and a miracle for Israel.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - No Egyptian records of a slave population, plagues, or a mass departure. Egypt recorded everything — including far smaller events - No evidence of 2 million people living in the Sinai for 40 years: no campsites, no graves, no pottery, no animal bones. The Sinai desert cannot support that many people - No evidence of conquest in Canaan that matches the biblical timeline. Many cities Joshua supposedly conquered (like Jericho and Ai) were either unoccupied or already destroyed centuries earlier - No demographic shift in Canaan that suggests an incoming population. The archaeological record shows continuous Canaanite habitation

card.title: The bottom line
card.content: Mainstream archaeologists and biblical historians (Israel Finkelstein, William Dever, Richard Elliott Friedman, and most others) agree that the Exodus as described in the Bible did not happen. Some suggest a small group of Semitic slaves may have escaped Egypt and their story was later magnified into a national epic. But the mass Exodus of millions is not supported by any evidence.

slide.notes: The Exodus is the most foundational story in the Old Testament. It's the event that defines Israel as a nation and establishes the covenant with God. If it didn't happen, the theological framework built on it -- the Law, the covenant, the promised land -- loses its historical anchor. It doesn't mean the stories are meaningless, but it means they are theology, not history.

slide.title: The Conquest
The Conquest of Canaan: What the Archaeology Reveals
slide.subtitle: The walls of Jericho fell -- but not when the Bible says.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: Joshua's army crosses the Jordan, destroys Jericho as its walls fall, and conquers Canaan city by city, wiping out entire populations as God commanded. A swift, total, divinely ordained conquest.

Jericho
Excavated by Kathleen Kenyon. Destroyed around **1550 BCE** -- **300 years before** the biblical date (~1200 BCE). By 1200 BCE it was a small, unfortified settlement or uninhabited.

Ai
The name means "the ruin" -- fittingly, it was already a ruin when the Israelites supposedly conquered it. Abandoned centuries before.

No Coordinated Conquest
Cities Joshua supposedly destroyed show no evidence of a coordinated campaign. Some were destroyed at different times, others not destroyed at all.

Canaanite Emergence Model
The consensus: Israelites did not invade Canaan -- they **emerged from within** Canaanite society. The first "Israelite" settlements appear ~1200 BCE with material culture indistinguishable from Canaanites.

card.title: The bottom line
card.content: The Israelites did not invade Canaan from outside -- they **were** Canaanites who gradually differentiated themselves. The conquest narrative was written centuries later as a theological origin myth, not a historical record.

slide.notes: The conquest narrative is one of the most morally problematic parts of the Bible -- God commanding genocide. The archaeological evidence suggests this never happened, which is both a relief and a revelation. It means the genocide was not historical fact but theological fiction. But it also means the Bible presents morally abhorrent commands that were never actually given -- they were written to serve a political purpose.

slide.title: Historical Conclusion
What the Evidence Shows
slide.subtitle: The pattern is consistent and devastating.

card.title: 🌊 Noah's Flood
card.content: No geological evidence for a global flood in the last 6,000 years. Ice cores show 100,000+ years of uninterrupted annual layers. The story derives from older Mesopotamian flood myths.

card.title: 🇪🇬 The Exodus
card.content: No Egyptian records of a slave population, plagues, or mass departure. No archaeological evidence of 2 million people in the Sinai for 40 years. The scholarly consensus: the Exodus as described did not happen.

card.title: ⚔️ The Conquest
card.content: Jericho was destroyed 300 years before the biblical date. Ai was already a ruin. The Israelites did not invade Canaan -- they emerged from within Canaanite society.

card.title: The verdict:
card.content: In every case where independent evidence exists to test the Bible's historical claims, the evidence fails to support them. The most parsimonious explanation is that these stories were written centuries after the supposed events, as theological and political constructs -- not as history. This does not make them worthless, but it means the Bible is not a reliable historical record.

slide.notes: The pattern is clear. Each of these stories was written centuries after the events they describe, by authors with clear theological and political motivations. The archaeological evidence consistently tells a different story. This doesn't mean the stories are meaningless -- they are powerful expressions of Israelite identity and faith. But they are not history. And if the Bible's foundational narratives are not historically reliable, the claim that it is a divinely inspired record of God's actions in the world is severely weakened.

slide.title: Section Jesus
The Case of Jesus
slide.subtitle: What can history tell us about Jesus? And do the New Testament's claims about him hold up?
slide.notes: Jesus of Nazareth is the central figure of Christianity. This section examines what historians can affirm about the historical Jesus, whether the resurrection claim is credible, how the New Testament uses Old Testament prophecies, and whether Jesus's own predictions about the future came true.

slide.title: Jesus Intro
What Can We Know About Jesus?
slide.subtitle: Three questions: Is the resurrection credible? Were the prophecies really predictions? Did Jesus's own promises come true?

card.title: The Claim
card.content: Christianity stands or falls on the resurrection. If Jesus rose from the dead, Christianity is true. If he did not, it is false. Paul himself makes this clear: "If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile" (1 Cor 15:17). This is the claim we must examine most carefully -- and by the standards of historical evidence, it requires extraordinary proof.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: Christians often point to Old Testament prophecies as evidence that Jesus was the messiah. But do those verses actually predict Jesus, or were they reinterpreted after the fact? And Jesus himself made specific predictions about his own return within his disciples' lifetime -- predictions that did not come true. This section examines all three questions.

slide.notes: The Jesus section covers three distinct but related lines of evidence: (1) whether the resurrection is historically credible, (2) whether OT prophecies were genuinely predictive or retrofitted, and (3) whether Jesus's own predictions about the future were accurate. Each alone is significant; together they form a coherent picture.

slide.title: Resurrection
The Resurrection: Extraordinary Claim, Insufficient Evidence
slide.subtitle: The central claim of Christianity -- and the hardest to verify historically.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: A man died, was dead for three days, and then rose from the dead -- never to die again -- resurrected to a glorified, immortal body. This is a miracle of the highest order, and it requires correspondingly high-quality evidence.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - The empty tomb story appears only in the Gospels, decades later - Paul's account (1 Cor 15) mentions only visions, not an empty tomb - Paul claims 500 witnesses saw the resurrected Jesus (1 Cor 15:6), yet names not one of them — and no contemporary historian corroborates the mass sighting - The Gospel accounts contradict each other on who found the tomb, what they saw, and what happened next - Natural explanations (hallucination, borrowed tomb, wrong tomb, legend formation) are more parsimonious than a violation of every known law of nature - No contemporary non-Christian source mentions it - No extra-biblical accounts exist of the Gospel miracles — tombs opening (Matt 27:52-53), feeding 5,000, darkness at noon — all in a Roman-governed province, yet unrecorded by any contemporary historian

slide.notes: The resurrection is the keystone of Christianity. Paul says if Christ didn't rise, faith is futile. So the evidence matters enormously. What we have: four contradictory accounts written decades later by anonymous authors, no independent corroboration from Roman or Jewish sources, and Paul -- our earliest source -- mentions only visions, not a physical tomb. Historians can establish that some early Christians believed Jesus appeared to them, but establishing that a dead man actually rose requires evidence of a different order entirely.

slide.title: OT Prophecies Intro
The Prophecy Problem
slide.subtitle: Christians claim dozens of Old Testament verses predict Jesus. But do they actually?

card.title: The Claim
card.content: The New Testament authors used a technique called **vaticinium ex eventu** -- reading earlier texts in light of later events. Verses that originally referred to contemporary figures (King Ahaz, the nation of Israel, the Psalmist's own suffering) were reinterpreted as "prophecies" of Jesus. This was standard Jewish interpretive practice at the time, but it is not prediction in any meaningful sense.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - Isaiah 7:14 "virgin will conceive” — Hebrew word almah means "young woman" not "virgin." Referred to Isaiah's own son, born during the Syro-Ephraimite war. - Micah 5:2 "Bethlehem" — refers to a coming ruler who would defend Israel against Assyria. Jesus was born in Bethlehem, but the prophecy was about a contemporary deliverer. - Hosea 11:1 "out of Egypt I called my son" — refers to the nation of Israel, not an individual. Matthew takes it out of context entirely. - Jeremiah 31:15 "Rachel weeping" — refers to the Babylonian exile, not a massacre by Herod. Matthew recontextualizes it to fit his narrative. - Isaiah 53 "Suffering Servant" — describes the nation of Israel or Isaiah himself, not an individual messiah. Jewish interpretation has never read it as messianic. - Psalm 22 "my God, my God" — a poetic psalm describing the Psalmist's own suffering. The "pierced" detail is a mistranslation of "like a lion." - Psalm 16:10 "not abandoned to the grave" — the Psalmist expresses confidence in God's protection, not a prediction of resurrection.

slide.notes: The prophecy argument is one of the most commonly used by apologists. When you actually read each prophecy in its original context, you find that almost none of them are predictive in nature. They were about events and people contemporary to the writers. See the appendix for a detailed analysis of all seven prophecies.

slide.title: Prophecy Summary
What the Prophecies Actually Show
slide.subtitle: The pattern is clear and consistent across all major "messianic prophecies."

card.title: The Claim
card.content:
- The Old Testament contains dozens of specific predictions about a coming messiah
- Jesus fulfilled every one of them
- This proves Jesus was the prophesied messiah
- Old Testament prophecy is evidence of divine inspiration

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - Verses are consistently taken out of their original context - Original meanings refer to contemporary figures, events, or the nation of Israel - "Fulfillment" is often vague, metaphorical, or simply incorrect - Many prophecies cited by the NT are not predictive at all in their original setting

slide.notes: After examining the ten most-cited messianic prophecies, the pattern is unmistakable. Each one requires ignoring the original context, changing the meaning of words, or reinterpreting poetry as prediction.

slide.title: Failed Predictions Intro
When Prophecy Fails
slide.subtitle: Jesus made specific, testable predictions about the future. They did not come true.

card.content: If a prophet makes a prediction and it does not come true, Deuteronomy 18:22 is clear: "That prophet has presumed to speak in my name… you need not be afraid of him." Jesus made several predictions with clear timeframes. They are the most difficult passages in the New Testament for Christian apologists, and entire books have been written attempting to explain them away. Let's examine what Jesus actually predicted and what actually happened.

slide.notes: These aren't obscure passages. They're some of the most clearly stated predictions in the Gospels. If Jesus was wrong about his own timeline, that raises profound questions about everything else he taught.

slide.title: Second Coming Generation
Return Within a Generation
slide.subtitle: The most explicit and most problematic prediction.

card.title: What Jesus Said
card.content:
**Matthew 16:28:** "There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom."
**Matthew 24:30-34:** "They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory… Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place."
**Mark 13:30:** "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place."
**Mark 9:1:** "Some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God come with power."

card.title: The Reality
card.content: Every single person of that generation died. The Son of Man did not return. "This generation" cannot be redefined to mean "the Jewish people" or "the generation that sees the signs" without violating the plain meaning of the text. Albert Schweitzer, Bart Ehrman, E.P. Sanders, and most critical scholars agree: Jesus expected the end within his own lifetime and was mistaken.

slide.notes: Apologists try to redefine "this generation" as "this race" (the Jews) or "the generation that sees these signs." But in every other Gospel context, "this generation" clearly means the living contemporaries. This is the most well-documented failed prediction in the Bible.

slide.title: 12 Thrones
The Twelve Apostles on Thrones
slide.subtitle: A specific promise to his closest followers.

card.title: What Jesus Said
card.content: **Matthew 19:28:** "Truly I tell you, at the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."

card.title: The Reality
card.content: None of the twelve apostles ever sat on a throne judging anyone. Most died in obscurity. Peter was crucified, James was executed, John died in exile, Judas committed suicide. The "renewal of all things" never occurred in their lifetimes. This is not a prediction that can be "spiritualized" -- thrones and judgment are concrete images with a concrete meaning.

slide.notes: Jesus promised his inner circle positions of power and authority. They died poor, persecuted, and executed. Either Jesus was wrong about the timing, or the promise was never fulfilled.

slide.title: Mission Promise
The Mission Promise
slide.subtitle: "You will not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes."

card.title: What Jesus Said
card.content: **Matthew 10:23:** "When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. For truly I tell you, you will not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes." Jesus is sending his disciples on a mission and telling them it will be interrupted by his return -- the ultimate interruption. The timeframe is explicit: before they finish their circuit of Israelite towns.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: The disciples finished going through Israel many times over. Paul traveled extensively throughout the region. The Son of Man did not come. Apologists argue that this was about the specific mission in Matthew 10 and that the "coming of the Son of Man" refers to Jesus's resurrection or the destruction of Jerusalem. But the text says nothing about resurrection or 70 CE -- it says the Son of Man will come before they finish their circuit.

slide.notes: This is one of the clearest time-bound predictions. The Son of Man was supposed to come before the disciples finished traveling through Israel. They finished traveling. He did not come.

slide.title: Failed Predictions Summary
If the Prophet Failed
slide.subtitle: If Jesus was wrong about his own return, why trust him on anything else?

card.title: Minimal Facts
card.content:
- Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish apocalyptic preacher
- He believed the end of the world was imminent
- He predicted his return within his disciples' lifetime
- His followers adapted after the prediction failed

card.title: The Dilemma
card.content:
- Jesus predicted his return within a generation -- it did not happen
- He promised his apostles thrones -- they did not receive them
- He guaranteed prayer works -- mountains stay put
- The most important prediction failed. What remains?

slide.notes: Scholars like Albert Schweitzer concluded that Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet who expected the kingdom of God to arrive imminently. He was wrong. If he was wrong about the central element of his own message, the foundation of Christian theology is shaken.

slide.title: Jesus Conclusion
The Verdict on Jesus
slide.subtitle: Three independent lines of evidence -- three consistent results.

card.title: ✝️ The Resurrection
card.content: No contemporary corroboration. Four contradictory Gospel accounts written decades later by anonymous authors. Paul's earlier account mentions only visions, not an empty tomb. Natural explanations are more parsimonious than a violation of every known law of nature.

card.title: 📖 OT Prophecies
card.content: Every major "messianic prophecy" fails under scrutiny. Verses are taken out of context, mistranslated, or refer to contemporary figures and events. The NT authors used **vaticinium ex eventu** -- reading earlier texts in light of later events.

card.title: ⏳ Jesus's Own Predictions
card.content: Jesus predicted his return within his disciples' lifetime ("this generation will not pass away"). He promised the apostles thrones. He said the Son of Man would come before they finished their mission. None of it happened. Deuteronomy says a prophet whose words fail is not from God.

**The verdict:** The New Testament's claims about Jesus fail on all three fronts. The resurrection lacks credible historical evidence, the prophecies are retrofitted rather than predictive, and Jesus's own predictions demonstrably did not come true. The most parsimonious explanation: Jesus was an apocalyptic preacher who was wrong about the timing of the end, and his followers adapted his message after his death.

slide.notes: Historians largely agree that a historical Jesus existed. What they do not agree on is the supernatural framework built around him. The consensus among secular historians is that the Gospel accounts contain legendary embellishment, that the resurrection lacks the evidence needed to establish such an extraordinary event, and that Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet who expected the end within his own lifetime and was mistaken. The prophecies and failed predictions only reinforce this picture.

slide.title: Section Moral
The Moral Argument
slide.subtitle: Does Christian morality stand up to philosophical scrutiny? And does the Bible itself provide a sound moral foundation?
slide.notes: The moral argument in Christianity usually takes two forms. First, that objective morality requires God. Second, that the Bible provides a moral foundation. We'll examine both, and see how they stack up against secular moral philosophy.

slide.title: Moral Intro
Does Christianity Provide a Sound Moral Foundation?
slide.subtitle: Two questions: Is the Bible's moral teaching defensible? And are its core doctrines just?

card.title: What the Bible Commands
card.content: The Old Testament contains laws endorsing slavery, genocide, and capital punishment for offenses like working on the Sabbath. Women were treated as property. These are presented as God's direct commands, not cultural concessions. If the Bible is a divine moral guide, its commands should be morally exemplary. But by modern standards, much of it is not.

card.title: What Christian Doctrine Requires
card.content: Beyond the specific commands, the core doctrines of Christianity raise deeper moral questions. Is it just to punish finite sins with infinite suffering? Is it fair to hold all humanity guilty for Adam's transgression? Is a blood sacrifice a morally coherent way to achieve forgiveness? These are not theological puzzles -- they are questions about whether the Christian system is fundamentally just.

slide.notes: We will examine both the specific moral teachings of the Bible and the broader moral framework of Christian doctrine. The goal is not to compare Christianity to an impossible standard, but to ask: does it provide a moral foundation that is coherent, just, and defensible?

slide.title: OT Slavery and Genocide
Biblical Morality: Slavery & Genocide
slide.subtitle: The Old Testament condones -- and God commands -- practices we now consider among the worst moral evils.

card.title: 🔗 Slavery
card.content:
The Bible does not condemn slavery -- it regulates and endorses it. Key passages:
**Leviticus 25:44-46** -- God tells Israel they may buy slaves from surrounding nations and pass them as inherited property to their children. These slaves are owned for life, unlike Hebrew servants who go free after six years. **Exodus 21:20-21** -- If a master beats a slave to death, he is punished only if the slave dies **immediately**. If the slave lingers for a day or two, the master is not punished because the slave is his property. **Ephesians 6:5** -- The New Testament tells slaves to obey their masters with fear and trembling, as they would Christ. Nowhere in either testament is slavery condemned as a moral evil.

card.title: Genocide
card.content:
God explicitly commands the wholesale destruction of entire peoples:
**Deuteronomy 20:16-18** -- "In the cities of the nations the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance, do not leave alive anything that breathes. Completely destroy them... so that they will not teach you to follow all the detestable things they do for their gods." **1 Samuel 15:3** -- God commands Saul to "attack the Amalekites and totally destroy everything that belongs to them. Do not spare them; put to death men and women, children and infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys." Saul is later *rejected as king* for sparing the Amalekite king and the best livestock. **Joshua 6:21** -- The army of Israel "devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword." This is presented as obedience to divine command, not a regrettable act of war.

card.title: The Apologetic Response
card.content: That was the Old Covenant; we're under the New Covenant." But this raises a serious problem: if God's moral commands can change, then morality is not absolute -- it is relative to whatever God commands at the time. And it means God once commanded slavery and genocide, which we now recognize as evil. Did God change his mind? Or did human moral understanding surpass what scripture presents as divine will?

slide.notes: The slavery and genocide passages are the most morally problematic parts of the Bible. The common defence is the Old/New Covenant distinction, but this is theologically problematic: if God's moral commands changed, then either God changed his mind (contradicting Malachi 3:6), or those commands were never absolute moral truths. Moreover, the New Testament doesn't condemn slavery either -- it tells slaves to obey their masters.

slide.title: OT Misogyny and Capital Punishment
Biblical Morality: Misogyny & Capital Punishment
slide.subtitle: The Bible treats women as property and prescribes the death penalty for minor offences.

card.title: Misogyny in the Bible
card.content: Women are consistently treated as second-class citizens throughout scripture — and this is presented as God's design, not human corruption. Daughters could be sold into slavery (Exodus 21:7), women were considered property (the Ten Commandments list wives alongside oxen and donkeys), and female testimony was valued below male testimony in legal matters. Paul writes that women should remain silent in churches (1 Cor 14:34-35) and that man is the head of woman (1 Cor 11:3). These are not cultural asides — they are presented as divine order.

card.title: Capital Punishment for Minor Offences
card.content: The Old Testament prescribes death for working on the Sabbath (Exodus 31:14-15), cursing parents (Leviticus 20:9), adultery (Leviticus 20:10), homosexuality (Leviticus 20:13), and prophesying falsely (Deuteronomy 18:20). These laws are presented alongside the Ten Commandments as God's direct commands. Christians today pick and choose which apply, but the text itself makes no such distinction — it presents a single, unified legal code from God.

card.title: The Apologetic Problem
card.content: Christians often dismiss these as "Old Covenant" laws. But this means either (a) God's moral commands changed (contradicting Malachi 3:6), or (b) those were never absolute moral truths. It also means God once commanded death for Sabbath-breaking — which we now recognize as monstrous. Did God change his mind, or did human moral understanding surpass what scripture presents as divine will?

slide.notes: The death penalty passages are often hand-waved as belonging to the Old Covenant, but the same Bible elevates these laws alongside the Ten Commandments. Christians who pick and choose which Old Testament laws apply are doing exactly what the Bible says they shouldn't -- selectively following a supposedly divine moral code. The misogyny passages are equally troubling: women are consistently treated as second-class citizens, and this is presented as God's design, not human corruption.

slide.title: Hell and Eternal Punishment
Hell: The Problem of Eternal Punishment
slide.subtitle: Finite sin, infinite punishment -- is that justice?

card.title: The Traditional Doctrine
card.content: Mainstream Christianity has historically taught that those who die without accepting Jesus as savior will suffer eternal, conscious torment in hell. This is not annihilation -- it is forever. The suffering never ends. And it applies not just to murderers and tyrants, but to good people who happened to be born into the wrong religion, or who honestly could not believe.

card.title: The Moral Problem
card.content: - Proportionality: Every criminal justice system in the world punishes crimes proportionally. A lifetime of sin — even a very bad one — cannot justify infinite suffering. No finite crime deserves infinite punishment. If a human judge sentenced someone to eternal torture for stealing bread, we'd call it monstrous. Why does God get a pass? - Finite creatures, infinite debt: The theological defense is that sin against an infinite God incurs infinite debt. But this is an invented metric — it assumes the nature of the offended party determines the magnitude of the crime. The scale of punishment should fit the crime, not the perceived status of the victim. - Knowledge problem: Billions of people — including children who die young, those in remote tribes, and sincere followers of other faiths — are condemned for not believing something they had no reasonable chance of believing. Is ignorance a sin worthy of eternal torment? - Annihilation vs. torment: Some Christians reject eternal conscious torment in favor of annihilationism. This is more defensible but still problematic — it means God creates beings knowing they will be destroyed, which is hard to reconcile with a loving creator.

slide.notes: Hell is one of the most difficult doctrines in Christianity. In recent decades, many Christians have moved away from the traditional view of eternal conscious torment toward annihilationism or universalism. But the traditional view remains the majority position globally, and it was the dominant view for most of church history. If hell is not eternal conscious torment, then what exactly did Jesus save us from? And if it is, then the moral problem is profound: an all-powerful God who could simply annihilate sinners or rehabilitate them instead chooses to torture them forever. This is not justice by any reasonable definition.

slide.title: Original Sin
Original Sin: Born Guilty
slide.subtitle: The doctrine that we are all born sinful -- and therefore deserve punishment -- before we have done anything wrong.

card.title: The Doctrine
card.content: Augustine codified the doctrine of original sin: because Adam sinned, all of humanity inherits both a sinful nature and the guilt of that first sin. We are born **already guilty** in God's eyes, deserving of punishment before we've committed a single wrong act. This is why infant baptism was considered necessary in much of church history -- unbaptized babies who died were thought to go to hell or to a separate place called limbo.

card.title: The Injustice
card.content: - Inherited guilt: In what moral system does guilt pass from parent to child? We do not hold children responsible for their parents' crimes. The very idea is repugnant to any sense of justice. Yet this is exactly what original sin claims: you are guilty of Adam's sin, and you deserve punishment for it, through no choice of your own. - Inherited nature: Even the milder version — that we inherit a sinful nature rather than guilt — is troubling. It means God created beings with a built-in inclination to sin, then punishes them for acting on that inclination. It is like creating someone with an addiction and then condemning them for using. - The escape clause: The solution, according to Christianity, is Jesus. But this means God required a blood sacrifice of himself to himself to fix a problem he created in the first place. If God can forgive sins freely — and he is said to be perfectly loving and merciful — why is a sacrifice necessary at all? Why not just forgive? - Substitutionary atonement: The idea that an innocent person must be punished for the guilty is an ancient tribal concept (scapegoating), not a model of justice. In any civilized legal system, punishing an innocent person for the crimes of the guilty is called a miscarriage of justice.

slide.notes: Original sin is the theological linchpin of Pauline Christianity. Without it, there is no need for atonement, no need for a savior, and no need for Christianity itself. Jesus's mission only makes sense if humanity is in a state of sin from which it cannot rescue itself. If the doctrine of original sin is morally indefensible -- and it is -- then the entire soteriological framework built on it collapses.

slide.title: Moral Summary
The Moral Landscape
slide.subtitle: Christianity's core moral doctrines are indefensible. The Bible's specific commands are worse. Secular frameworks provide a more consistent foundation.

card.title: Doctrines
card.content: Hell (finite sin, infinite punishment) and original sin (inherited guilt) are morally incoherent. A blood sacrifice to appease divine wrath is a primitive concept, not a sophisticated ethical system.

card.title: Scripture
card.content: The Bible endorses slavery, genocide, and misogyny as divine commands — not cultural concessions. We've made moral progress despite the Bible, not because of it.

card.title: Conclusion
card.content: Secular frameworks grounded in empathy, reason, and human flourishing provide a more consistent moral foundation than divine command does.

slide.notes: The moral case against Christianity is not just that the Bible endorses outdated practices -- it's that the core doctrines of the faith are themselves morally problematic. Eternal punishment for finite sins is not justice. Inherited guilt for Adam's transgression is not how moral responsibility works. A blood sacrifice to appease divine wrath is a primitive concept, not a sophisticated ethical system. We've made moral progress despite the Bible's endorsement of slavery and genocide, not because of it. Secular frameworks -- grounded in empathy, reason, and human flourishing -- provide a more consistent foundation for morality than divine command does.

slide.title: Section Bible
The Bible Itself
slide.subtitle: Examining the Bible's own claims: inerrancy, canon, contradictions, and the problem of prophecy.
slide.notes: The Bible makes strong claims: it is the inspired, inerrant word of God. But when we examine it with critical tools -- textual criticism, source criticism, and internal consistency checks -- it looks exactly like a human book. If the Bible contains internal contradictions, misused prophecies, unfulfilled predictions, and a canon settled by fallible councils, then the claim of divine authorship fails.

slide.title: Bible Intro
Is the Bible What It Claims to Be?
slide.subtitle: The Bible claims to be the inspired, inerrant word of God. Does the evidence support that claim?

card.content: Protestant Christianity holds that the Bible is the inspired, inerrant Word of God -- without error in its original manuscripts and authoritative for faith and practice. This is a strong claim, and it is testable. If the Bible contains internal contradictions, historical errors, or signs of human invention, then the claim of divine authorship is undermined.

card.title: The Test
card.content: We will examine three areas: 1. Textual transmission -- do we even have the original text? 2. Canon formation -- who decided which books belong, and on what basis? 3. Internal consistency -- does the Bible contradict itself? The answers to these questions will tell us whether the Bible looks like a divinely inspired book or a very human one.

slide.notes: This section covers the Bible's own claims about itself. We examine the textual evidence for transmission, the historical process of canonization, and the internal consistency of the text itself. Each area independently tests the claim of divine authorship.

slide.title: Inerrancy & Textual Transmission
Inerrancy & Textual Transmission
slide.subtitle: The original autographs don't exist. What we have are copies of copies.

card.title: The Claim
card.content: Many Christians believe the Bible is without error in its original manuscripts. But we don't have the originals. We have thousands of handwritten copies, all of which contain differences -- scribal errors, additions, deletions, and theological corrections.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: - There are 400,000+ textual variants among NT manuscripts - Most are minor, but some affect doctrine: the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) and the longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) are later additions, not original - The Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7-8) -- the only explicit Trinitarian verse -- was added centuries later - We reconstruct the "original" text through scholarly inference, but we can never be certain we have it exactly right

card.title: The Bottom Line
card.content: Beyond the textual issues above, there's a logical one: the Bible cannot be used as evidence for the Bible's own reliability. When Christians cite 2 Timothy 3:16 ("All Scripture is God-breathed") to prove inerrancy, they're appealing to the very book whose reliability is in question. The Quran claims it is the perfect word of God. The Book of Mormon claims divine origin. Every scripture can assert its own authority -- that doesn't make it true.

slide.notes: If God wanted to preserve an inerrant text for humanity, why didn't he preserve the originals? Why did he allow thousands of scribal errors to accumulate? Why are key passages that support important doctrines later additions? The inerrancy doctrine requires faith not just in the original text, but in the process of transmission and the ability of scholars to reconstruct that text. That's a lot of faith in a very human process.

slide.title: Canon Formation
The Canon: Chosen by Men, Not God
slide.subtitle: Who decided which books belong in the Bible?

card.title: 📜 The Old Testament Canon
card.content: Jesus and the NT authors used the Septuagint (Greek translation), which includes the Apocrypha/deuterocanonical books. Protestants later excluded these books. There was no "official" Jewish canon until the Council of Jamnia (~90 CE).

card.title: 📖 The New Testament Canon
card.content: The 27-book NT canon was not finalized until the late 4th century (Council of Carthage, 397 CE). Many gospels were circulated before being excluded: Thomas, Peter, Shepherd of Hermas, Didache. The canon was decided by fallible bishops and councils.

card.title: 🔍 Criteria for Inclusion
card.content: Books were included based on apostolic authorship, orthodoxy, and widespread usage -- human criteria, not divine markers. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions still disagree on the canon today.

slide.notes: The canon of scripture wasn't handed down from heaven -- it was a centuries-long process of debate, politics, and theological negotiation. Different churches had different Bibles. Marcion had his own canon. The Gnostics had theirs. The canon we have today reflects the winners of those theological battles, not a self-evident list of God-authored books. If the Bible is uniquely inspired, shouldn't its table of contents be obvious?

slide.title: Contradictions
Internal Contradictions
slide.subtitle: An inerrant book shouldn't contradict itself. Yet it does.

card.title: Historical Contradictions
card.content: Who killed Goliath? David (1 Sam 17) or Elhanan (2 Sam 21:19)? Who incited David's census? God (2 Sam 24:1) or Satan (1 Chr 21:1)? How did Judas die? Hanged himself (Matt 27:5) or fell and burst open (Acts 1:18)? When was the Last Supper? Before or during Passover? (Synoptics vs John) What happened at the empty tomb? One angel? Two? Sitting? Standing? Inside? Outside?

card.title: Theological Contradictions
card.content: Is salvation by faith alone (Eph 2:8-9) or faith + works (James 2:24)? Luther wanted to remove James. Does God repent/change his mind? Yes (Ex 32:14, Jon 3:10). No (Num 23:19, 1 Sam 15:29). Does God tempt people? Yes (Gen 22:1, 2 Sam 24:1). No (James 1:13). Is God a God of peace or does he create evil? (Isa 45:7 vs multiple "God is love" passages) Are we justified by faith alone or do we need to keep the law?

slide.notes: Apologists have answers for every contradiction. Harmonization is always possible if you're creative enough. But harmonization isn't the same as the plain reading of the text. When you need to invent elaborate explanations to reconcile two accounts that say different things, you're not discovering the text's meaning -- you're imposing a harmonization on it. An inerrant book would be self-consistent on its face.

slide.title: Fantastical Elements
Fantastical Elements in the Bible
slide.subtitle: The Bible contains supernatural events that defy credibility -- and their only source is the Bible itself.

card.title: 🐍 The Talking Snake
card.content: In Genesis 3, a serpent speaks to Eve and debates theology. Not a metaphor -- the story presents it as a literal conversation. In the ancient Near East, talking animals were a known literary trope (like Balaam's donkey in Numbers 22). These are folkloric elements, not historical reporting. No modern biologist or historian treats this as a credible event.

card.title: 🐴 Balaam's Talking Donkey
card.content: Numbers 22:28-30: a donkey speaks to Balaam in Hebrew. Like the serpent, this is a fable-like episode. The story even includes the donkey arguing logically with its owner. The Rabbis themselves recognized this as a special creation for that moment -- acknowledging it is not a normal event. The folkloric character is unmistakable.

card.title: ☀️ The Sun Standing Still
card.content: Joshua 10:12-14: Joshua commands the sun to stand still "about a whole day" so the Israelites can finish a battle. If the sun literally stopped in the sky, the laws of physics would be catastrophically violated -- the Earth's rotation would fling everything eastward at hundreds of miles per hour. No other culture recorded this event, yet it would have been visible across half the planet. This is clearly a poetic exaggeration of a military victory, not a historical report.

card.title: The bottom line
card.content: Stories that would be instantly dismissed as folklore in any other context are treated as literal history when found in the Bible. These elements follow the conventions of ancient myth and legend -- not of history writing. If a talking snake appeared in the Quran or the Book of Mormon, skeptics would rightly point out its implausibility. Consistency demands the same standard for the Bible.

slide.notes: The presence of fantastical elements is a strong indicator that we're reading mythology, not history. Talking animals, the sun halting in the sky, a worldwide flood, people living 900+ years -- these are the hallmarks of ancient storytelling, not reliable historical records. Every other culture's sacred texts are held to this standard. Why should the Bible be exempt?

slide.title: OT Reinterpretation
Theological Reinterpretation of History
slide.subtitle: The Old Testament often reinterprets ordinary events as divine acts -- a pattern visible when compared to other ancient sources.

card.title: The Pattern
card.content: Throughout the Old Testament, ordinary historical events are recast as direct divine interventions. Military victories become miracles. Natural disasters become divine punishment. Diplomatic treaties become commands of God. This was standard practice in the ancient Near East — every nation credited its gods with its successes and blamed them for its failures. The Bible does the same, but later readers took these poetic interpretations literally.

card.title: Concrete Examples
card.content: - The Exodus: A small group of Semitic slaves escaping Egypt becomes a foundational miracle of 2 million people crossing the Red Sea. Egyptian records of the period — which meticulously document far smaller events — record nothing. - The Conquest of Canaan: Archaeology shows the Israelites emerged from within Canaanite society. The biblical account of miraculous military conquest was written centuries later as a theological origin myth. - Sennacherib's Invasion (701 BCE): Assyrian records describe Hezekiah paying tribute. The Bible (2 Kings 19) credits divine intervention, claiming an angel killed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers overnight. No Assyrian record mentions this — because it didn't happen. - The sun standing still at Gibeon (Joshua 10): A poetic description of a long day of battle, taken literally by later readers. No other ancient source records this event, and the physics alone makes it scientifically impossible.

card.title: The Bottom Line
card.content: The Bible authors were theologians writing theology, not historians writing journalism. When modern Christians insist that every poetic description of divine intervention is literally and historically true, they are misunderstanding the genre of the text. Every other culture's sacred writings are recognized as theological interpretations of history — the Bible deserves the same critical treatment.

slide.notes: The reinterpretation of history is not unique to the Bible -- it was the standard way ancient peoples understood their world. But when modern Christians insist that every poetic description of divine intervention is literally and historically true, they are misunderstanding the genre of the text. The Bible authors were theologians writing theology, not historians writing journalism.

slide.title: Bible Objections
Common Defense Arguments
slide.subtitle: Christians often defend the Bible with these arguments -- each fails under scrutiny.
slide.notes: These are the most common Christian apologetic arguments for the Bible's authority. Each is presented as its advocates state it, followed by the critical response.

slide.title: Objection Authorship
"The Bible Is Unique in Authorship"
slide.subtitle: A common claim about the Bible's composition -- and why it doesn't hold up.

card.content: Around forty writers across 1,500 years -- kings, prophets, fishermen, a physician -- produced 66 books that share a unified theme of salvation through Jesus. No other religious text spans such diversity of authorship with such coherence.

card.title: Response
card.content: Writers from the same culture and shared history naturally produce coherent narratives. Yet even then, the Bible shows discrepancies: early texts use the plural **elohim**, betraying polytheistic origins; God's nature evolves from a violent tribal war god to a universal loving god; and the Bible contradicts itself on whether God creates evil (Isaiah 45:7 says yes, 1 John 1:5 says no). Coherence within a tradition is expected -- it's not evidence of divine origin.

slide.title: Objection Content
"The Bible Is Unique in Content"
slide.subtitle: Salvation by grace, not works -- is being different enough?

card.content: Unlike other religions that teach salvation through good works, the Bible uniquely offers salvation as a free gift through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8--9). No other sacred text claims a religious leader rose from the dead or gives assurance of eternal life.

card.title: Response
card.content: Uniqueness is not proof of truth. Geocentrism was unique. Alchemy was unique. The geocentric model of the solar system was unique. A claim being distinctive doesn't make it true -- it still requires evidence. Many religions offer unique salvation narratives; the question is not which is most different, but which is most supported by evidence.

slide.title: Objection Eyewitnesses
"The Gospels Were Written by Eyewitnesses"
slide.subtitle: Are the Gospels reliable firsthand accounts?

card.title: The Claim
card.content: The New Testament was written by eyewitnesses to the events soon after they took place, within the first century. The Gospels preserve the testimony of those who saw Jesus' ministry, death, and resurrection firsthand.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: The first gospel (Mark) was written some 40 years after Jesus' death -- decades of oral tradition during which stories change, embellish, and distort with every transmission. The Gospels are anonymous; their traditional author names were assigned later. Eyewitness testimony is notoriously unreliable even in controlled modern settings. Ancient accounts, especially those written decades later by non-eyewitnesses, must be treated with appropriate skepticism.

slide.title: Objection Manuscripts
"The Manuscript Evidence Is Overwhelming"
slide.subtitle: More copies means more reliable -- or does it?

card.title: The Claim
card.content: The New Testament has over 5,300 Greek manuscripts, 10,000 Latin, and 9,000 other copies -- far more than any other ancient work. By comparison, Aristotle's **Poetics** survives in only five manuscripts, the earliest over a thousand years after the original.

card.title: The Reality
card.content: A large number of manuscripts reflects that Christianity was popular and institutionally organized, not that it's true. The Quran has few early manuscripts because Islamic leaders controlled the process and burned variant copies -- that says nothing about its truth or falsehood. A falsehood repeated many times does not become true. The question is not how many copies exist, but whether the original events actually happened.

slide.title: Objection Changed Lives
"The Bible Changes Lives"
slide.subtitle: Are transformed lives evidence that Christianity is true?

card.title: The Claim
card.content: Countless people around the world testify to freedom from addiction, destructive lifestyles, and despair through following biblical principles and faith in Christ. God's Word produces transformed lives (Isaiah 55:11).

card.title: The Reality
card.content: Beliefs changing lives happens in every religion -- Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, and secular humanists all report transformed lives. If changed lives are evidence, they're evidence for all ideologies, which means they're evidence for none. And if we judge by fruits, we must also account for the Inquisition, the Crusades, and fallen leaders like Ravi Zacharias and Kong Hee -- evil done in Christ's name using the same Bible as justification.

slide.title: Bible Summary
The Bible as a Human Book
slide.subtitle: Examined critically, the Bible looks like a human book — not a divinely inspired inerrant text.

card.title: Textual Transmission
card.content: No original manuscripts exist. We have copies of copies with 400,000+ variants. Key passages (John 7:53-8:11, Mark 16:9-20, 1 John 5:7-8) are later additions.

card.title: Canon & Consistency
card.content: The canon was settled by fallible councils centuries later. The Bible contradicts itself on historical details and contains fantastical elements (talking snakes, demons in pigs) that defy credibility.

card.title: Defenses Fail
card.content: Common apologetic arguments — unity of authorship, manuscript evidence, changed lives, eyewitness testimony — fail under scrutiny or apply equally to other scriptures.

slide.notes: When you examine the Bible with the same critical tools you'd apply to any ancient text, it looks exactly like what you'd expect from a collection of human writings: reflecting the cultures, biases, limitations, and theological agendas of their authors. The simplest explanation for the Bible's features is not that it's a divinely inspired inerrant text, but that it's a very human book -- a remarkable one, to be sure, but human nonetheless.

slide.title: Section Philosophical
Philosophical Objections
slide.subtitle: Broader philosophical issues with the Christian worldview.
slide.notes: Beyond science, history, morality, and the Bible itself, there are broader philosophical problems with Christian theology. These aren't knock-down arguments, but they contribute to the cumulative case that Christianity fails as a coherent worldview.

slide.title: Philosophical Intro
Broader Problems with the Christian Worldview
slide.subtitle: Beyond science, history, and the Bible itself, Christianity faces fundamental philosophical challenges.

card.title: Internal Problems
card.content: Some problems arise from within Christian theology itself: the paradox of free will versus divine foreknowledge, the Euthyphro dilemma about the foundation of morality, and the logical problem of how a perfectly good God could create a world containing evil. These are not objections from outside -- they are contradictions between the attributes Christianity ascribes to God and the world we actually observe.

card.title: External Problems
card.content: Other problems come from how Christianity engages with the broader world: the unreliability of faith as a method for determining truth, the failure of Pascal's Wager as a pragmatic argument for belief, and the problem of divine hiddenness -- why a God who desires a relationship with us would remain so elusive. These challenges apply not just to Christianity but to any religious claim based on faith rather than evidence.

slide.notes: The philosophical objections are often the most abstract but also the most persistent. They don't rely on any particular scientific discovery or historical finding -- they ask whether the Christian worldview is coherent on its own terms.

slide.title: Euthyphro Dilemma
The Euthyphro Dilemma
slide.subtitle: Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it's good?

card.title: Horn 1: Divine Command
card.content: If good = whatever God commands, then morality is arbitrary. If God commanded genocide, slavery, or child sacrifice, those would be morally good by definition. This makes morality a matter of divine whim, not objective truth.

card.title: Horn 2: Independent Standard
card.content: If God commands good because it is independently good, then goodness exists apart from God. God is not the source of morality -- He's just a messenger. In that case, we can access the same moral standard through reason and empathy without needing divine revelation.

slide.notes: The Euthyphro dilemma is ancient and devastating. If morality depends on God's commands, then whatever God commands is good -- including the genocides and slavery commanded in the Old Testament. Many Christians try to avoid this by saying "God's nature is good," but that just pushes the question back: is God's nature good because it happens to be God's nature, or because goodness is a standard God's nature meets?

slide.title: Pascal&amp;#x27;s Wager
Pascal's Wager: The Bet You Can't Win
slide.subtitle: "Believe in God because you have everything to gain and nothing to lose."

card.title: The Argument
card.content: Pascal argued that belief in God is the rational bet: if God exists, the believer gains infinite reward and avoids infinite punishment. If God doesn't exist, the believer loses little. The atheist, by contrast, risks infinite loss for finite gain.

card.title: Why It Fails
card.content: - The Many-Gods Objection: Which God do you bet on? Islam, Hinduism, Judaism, and hundreds of other religions each promise different rewards and punishments. Pascal's wager tells you to believe — but doesn't tell you what to believe. The logic applies equally to any god. - Faith isn't a light switch: You cannot choose to believe something genuinely. If you try to "believe" just as insurance, you haven't actually believed — and an omniscient God would see through it. - False dichotomy: The wager presents only two options (Christian theism vs. atheism), ignoring all other religious possibilities. With hundreds of competing truth claims, the "rational bet" becomes a lottery, not a logical deduction.

card.title: The Bottom Line
card.content: Pascal's Wager is almost universally rejected by philosophers and theologians. It treats faith as an insurance policy, which is the opposite of genuine religious commitment. And it completely ignores the problem of religious pluralism: which God, exactly, are you betting on?

slide.notes: Pascal's Wager is probably the most famous argument for belief, and it's almost universally rejected by philosophers and theologians alike. It treats faith as an insurance policy, which is arguably the opposite of what genuine religious commitment should be. And it ignores the problem of religious pluralism: which specific version of God do you bet on?

slide.title: Faith Not a Virtue
Faith Is Not a Virtue
slide.subtitle: Is believing without evidence a virtue or a vice?

card.title: Defining Faith
card.content:
Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as "the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen." In practice, this often means believing something despite insufficient evidence. If you had sufficient evidence, it wouldn't be faith -- it would be knowledge.
The problem: faith is a methodology that leads people to believe contradictory things. Muslims have faith in the Quran. Hindus have faith in the Vedas. Mormons have faith in the Book of Mormon. Faith alone can't distinguish truth from falsehood.

card.title: The Epistemic Problem
card.content:
